Viewspec Vantage

What 10.7 million W&B workspace and report specs are made of, what a limit would cost, and what cleaning up would reclaim. MT SaaS, snapshot 2026-10-13.

Room 1 · The brief

Workspace Vantage: what the hackathon asked, and what this exhibit answers.

Workspace Vantage was a hackathon project, October 13 to 15, 2026. The proposal asked two things of the viewspec data: how widely each workspace feature is used, and what a proposed limit would break, sized in workspaces, active workspaces, people and accounts. The app's events record which pages people open, not how those pages are configured, so both answers have to come from the stored documents. Every room that follows is read from those 10.7 million documents.

Escape Velocity

BriefTake a workflow or pipeline past where people thought it could go. Set the baseline, show the delta.

HereBaseline: the proposal expected the viewspec path to be slow and expensive on SaaS. Room 2 · Orientation

A viewspec is the JSON document behind every W&B workspace and report.

It records which runs a page shows and how: the runs-table filters, grouping and sort, every panel and section, and the page's settings. Gorilla stores it as an opaque blob in views.spec; the browser normalizes it into a table of parts, edits those, and writes the whole document back. It is flexible because nothing constrains it. It is a problem for the same reason.

How it moves through the app

Stored

One row per view in MySQL, the whole document in spec. From 8 MiB the blob moves to object storage and the column goes NULL. Above 128 MiB the save fails. type is an unconstrained string and nothing validates the document on write.

views
  id        17074768
  type      'project-view'
  name      'nw-…-w'
  spec      '{"section":{…}}'   -- LONGTEXT, or NULL
  updated_at 2026-09-29        -- 1 s precision

Normalized

On load the browser splits the tree into parts keyed by a fresh random id, and replaces each child with a ref. 25 part types, each with a hand-written normalize and denormalize pair.

parts.runSet['a1'] = {
  name: 'Run set',
  filtersRef:  {id: 'f9', type: 'filters'},
  sortRef:     {id: 's2', type: 'sort'},
  …
}
parts.filters['f9'] = {op: 'AND', filters: […]}

Read by components

Components follow refs by hand with usePart (137 call sites in 64 files). Rebuilding the nested object (useWhole) was banned in 2024: every edit anywhere produced new objects for every panel, so everything re-rendered.

const runSet  = usePart(props.runSetRef);
const filters = usePart(runSet.filtersRef);
const sort    = usePart(runSet.sortRef);

Saved back

Every save denormalizes the whole tree and writes the full document. The save path is meant to drop the refs, but older clients did not.

denormalize(sectionRef, {includeRefs: false})
→ UpsertView(type, name, spec)
The leak. 54% of stored line-plot panels still carry a ref. Refs are 74 GB of the 403 GB of MySQL specs up to 4 MB, and two code paths still write them today: the run-view panels denormalizer and report-draft panel grids.

Flexible, and unstructured

What the flexibility buys

  • 46panel types in the wild. 22 have a schema; 24 more appear in stored specs (Confusion Matrix, Rerun Viewer, Weave Traces…), and the app keeps unknown ones intact.
  • 31Slate element types in reports. A report is a document tree with panel grids inside it. New block types ship without a storage change.
  • 4kinds of writer. The web app, the wandb-workspaces SDK, the Reports API and ARIA all write the same JSON. No server deploy is needed for a client to add a field.
  • 8dynamic-key maps (customRunColors, columnVisible, panelConfigOverrides, …) and opaque subtrees (Weave graphs, Vega specs) that no fixed table schema would hold.
  • 86definitions emerged bottom-up. Generated from what is stored, every sampled spec passes: the shapes are consistent enough to be a contract.

What the lack of structure costs

  • 0checks on write. type is a free-form varchar; 15 distinct types are stored, including 20 specs of a type the app does not know. UpsertView stores the blob as-is.
  • 114 GBof fields the app never reads (22% of MySQL spec bytes). Normalizer refs, duplicated root fields, deprecated flags; 27% in specs over 4 MB.
  • 95.9%of panels in big specs are ones auto-generation would recreate. 283.8M of 296M panels in the 13,730 MySQL workspaces over 4 MB. The largest stores 737,797 panels.
  • 54levels deep: a filter leaf nested inside its own current field, 18,356 specs. Plus 7,316 "==" ops the app has no operator for, and 7 specs that are not JSON at all.
  • 288stored fields the TypeScript types do not declare, and 17 of 26 paired types allow values the generated schema rejects. Nobody owns the shape.

Room 3 · Blast radius

Input a proposed limit. Output what it costs.

Some workspace features are expensive by construction: filtering or grouping by a summary metric cannot use an index. Capping them would make the app faster, if we knew who we would break. Every multi-run workspace in MT SaaS is fingerprinted, so the distribution is known and a cap can be priced in workspaces, people and accounts.

By plan

Affected workspaces by the owning organization's plan, and the share of that plan's workspaces in the chosen scope.

  • Scope is the 6.95M project-view, sweep-view and group-view specs across MySQL and object storage. Run views are excluded: the app has redirected them to the project workspace since 2025-10-21. Reports are not workspaces.
  • Affected means the stored value is strictly greater than the limit (a cap of 3 group-by keys affects workspaces with 4 or more). "Disallow" modes count workspaces that use the field class at all. Stored counts undercount what users see for panels, since auto-generated panels are stripped before saving.
  • Active means the project had run activity in the 90 days before 2026-10-13 and neither it nor its entity is deleted. People are view owners (views.user_id), not everyone who opens the workspace; "logged in recently" is within the same 90 days. Accounts are the organizations owning the projects; ARR is the sum of active_arr over affected paid orgs, an upper bound on exposure.
  • Figures differ from the hackathon findings table by under 0.5% because this build pins all dates to the snapshot and excludes the 7 specs that are not valid JSON.

Room 4 · Cleanup simulator

What deleting, resetting and pruning would reclaim, and who would notice.

Every rule below was scored against all 10.7M specs: deletion by project state and plan, a reset that keeps every configured panel and drops the ones auto-generation recreates, and pruning to the lean schema. Totals are exact aggregates except object-storage pruning, which is estimated from a sample. The recommended path frees 584 GB; adding run views makes it 598 GB, 73% of the table.

Presets

Delete views on deleted projects

Project or entity is soft-deleted. Covers all view types.

Delete workspaces users already deleted

Deleting a saved workspace in the UI only renames its view to xnw-…; the row and spec stay. These are hidden everywhere in the app.

Delete run views

The app can't open run-view specs any more: since 2025-10-21 (#35567, server 0.76.0) a run's workspace URL redirects to the project workspace in single-run mode. Neither ARIA nor the wandb-workspaces SDK uses them. Like already-deleted workspaces, removing them loses nothing anyone can reach. Dedicated and on-prem instances older than 0.76.0 still use them.

Delete views on idle projects

Project last_active_at older than the threshold. Pick which plans and view types are eligible.

Delete huge idle workspaces

Any plan. Workspaces and run views only.

Reset and restore workspaces

Drop panels auto-generation recreates. Keep custom charts, multi-metric and tweaked plots, sweep defaults, run sets and settings. Simulated for every workspace spec, including those in object storage.

Prune to the lean schema

Conform each remaining spec to viewspec.lean.schema.json: drop persisted normalizer refs (ref, *Ref, *Refs), root fields the app never reads, and workspace section keys the loader drops. Applies after deletion and after any reset. Removes nothing a user configured.

Who loses data

Red: paid or active users lose data. Amber: academic users, recent users, or paying customers' staff lose data, or paid users' workspaces get reset (their configured panels are kept).

Spec size distribution

How many specs are larger than each size: what the browser downloads when a workspace or report opens. MySQL and object storage together, log scale. Offloaded specs keep their size under pruning here, so the large-spec counts after are an upper bound.

By plan

What each rule set removes or shrinks, by the owning org's plan.

Where the savings come from by project idle age

    • Plans come from the org that owns the view's project (dim_organizations). A paying customer's employee working in a personal project counts under their personal (usually expired-trial) org. The "owned by paid users" flag catches that case via dim_users.is_paid.
    • Active means the project had activity in the last 90 days. That tracks runs, not whether anyone opens the workspace.
    • Reset and restore is simulated per workspace for all 9.6M workspace specs: MySQL specs in BigQuery and locally, offloaded specs streamed from object storage. Weave panels are kept because their default config isn't known, so sizes after reset are an upper bound. Aggressive mode also drops default panels the user moved or hid. "Keep all" sections is the lasting saving: the app recreates and saves emptied sections on load. A reset spec under 8 MiB moves from object storage back into MySQL on its next save.
    • Run views (run-view) have been unreachable in the app since 2025-10-21: the run workspace URL redirects to the project workspace in single-run mode (#35335, #35567). Creation fell from about 77K a month to almost none, and only 10 were saved in the 90 days before the snapshot. Deleting them, like deleting xnw- workspaces, isn't counted as data loss.
    • Pruning conforms specs to the lean schema (schema/lean.py, schema/prune.py). It was run on every MySQL spec, alone and after each reset variant, so those numbers are exact: specs up to 4 MB in BigQuery (schema/run_pass3.py), larger ones locally. Object storage uses ratios by view kind from a random sample of 278 offloaded specs. A pruned spec under 8 MiB lives in MySQL; one at 8 MiB or more in object storage.
    • Bytes are spec characters (LENGTH(spec)). The whole table is 524.5 GB in BigQuery; 2.6 GB of that is other view types and columns, which no rule touches.
